title: Nested CE windows, read path and scrub path counted apart
claim: Aggregate the correctable-error stream over several nested lookbacks (the published baseline uses 15 minutes and 1 hour) at every prediction time, and keep read-origin and scrub-origin errors in separate columns rather than one total.
rationale: The starter-kit baseline emits read_ce_log_num / read_ce_count / all_ce_log_num / all_ce_count over a list of window sizes; M2-MFP generalises the same idea to multiple scales because a single window cannot show whether a rate is rising.
applicability: Any CE stream that distinguishes the error origin in error_type. Each window must fit inside the declared lookback, or the shortest window the model was trained on will not exist at inference time.
expected_effect: Medium to large. It is the representation the official pipeline scores with, and the difference between read and scrub traffic is not recoverable from the total afterwards.
risk: Windows multiply columns and streaming state. Most units are quiet, so the short windows are empty for almost every row: a rate over an empty window is undefined, not zero, and turning it into zero teaches the model that silence and absence are the same event.
impl_hint: for each prediction time t and window w, aggregate over the half-open interval [t-w, t): log count and summed Count per origin. Emit NaN rather than 0 for a window holding no row, and keep the window list in the config so it is hashed into the run.

title: Recency and burstiness carry what counts cannot
claim: Add time-since-last-error, mean log interval and a storm counter that fires on a streak of consecutive events, on top of the per-window counts.
rationale: The baseline computes log_happen_frequency as window size divided by row count and a storm counter over a consecutive-row streak (its default streak threshold is 10); two units with the same CE count are distinguishable only by when those errors arrived.
applicability: Units with more than a couple of rows in the lookback. The inter-arrival features are undefined for a single-row window.
expected_effect: Medium. It separates steady background traffic from an accelerating burst, which is the shape an operator acts on.
risk: The streak threshold is a tuned constant on one dataset; choosing it against the evaluation split leaks the answer through a hyper-parameter that looks like a feature.
impl_hint: compute streaks on the sorted per-unit event times, not on the sample grid; carry the last event time across chunk boundaries so a boundary does not look like a long interval.

title: Where the errors sit is a feature: cell, column, row, bank, device
claim: Classify each window by how far up the memory hierarchy the failing ids spread - one cell, several columns of one row, several rows, several banks, several devices - and keep the raw distinct-id counts alongside that class.
rationale: The baseline derives fault_mode_others / device / bank / row / column / cell from the number of distinct ids at each level; Yu 2023 reports that spatio-temporal error-bit patterns correlate strongly with uncorrectable errors; M2-MFP builds per-level binary matrices for the same reason.
applicability: Only where the id columns are populated and not anonymised into a constant. A released column that is always zero produces one mode for every unit and is worse than nothing.
expected_effect: Medium to large on the units that fail: a concentrated pattern says a region is dying, a scattered one says something else is wrong.
risk: The classes are mutually exclusive by construction, so the outermost level hides the inner ones, and a two-row window produces a confident-looking mode out of noise.
impl_hint: count distinct ids per level after dropping the placeholder value the release uses for unknown, emit both the counts and the derived one-hot, and never derive the mode from a window below a stated minimum row count.

title: Decode the parity field into bit, dq and burst populations
claim: Parse each correctable error's parity information into the number of failing bits, the set of failing dq lanes, the set of failing bursts and the largest gap inside each, and carry the distribution of those sizes over the window.
rationale: Yu 2023 measured up to 15 percent F1 improvement from spatio-temporal error-bit information that ordinary CE-counting discards; the baseline implements the same decomposition for a 4-dq by 8-burst DDR4 part, including per-value histograms.
applicability: Where the released columns still carry parity or error-bit detail. The dq and burst geometry is part-specific, so the same column means something else on another platform.
expected_effect: Large for the multi-bit failures that ECC cannot fix - which is exactly the event being predicted.
risk: Hard-coding the lane and burst counts from a DDR4 assumption silently truncates or mislabels another part; an unparsable parity string must not be counted as zero errors.
impl_hint: decode parity into a bit set, take populations over the declared lane and burst widths, and record the geometry as configuration so a second platform produces a different hash instead of a silently reused feature file.

title: Long-history properties, including the first observed error
claim: Do not truncate the history to the recent window: carry the time of the first observed correctable error for the unit and slow aggregates over months, because access to a faulty region is spread over time and a short window can miss it entirely.
rationale: Bogatinovski 2022 argues prior work truncated history to fit practical constraints and so lost signal, and that the first CE is itself informative about the degraded state.
applicability: Only if the full per-unit history is available at feature time for every unit, including healthy ones. A feature that is computable for failed units and not for healthy ones leaks the label.
expected_effect: Medium, and dataset-dependent: it matters most when the recent window is empty, which is most rows.
risk: On a short default lookback the long-history columns are near-constant and add nothing while still costing a pass over the whole dataset; the cost is paid whether or not the gain arrives.
impl_hint: compute first-seen and lifetime counts in a separate cheap pass keyed by unit digest, so the bounded streaming feature pass does not have to hold the whole history.

title: Static hardware identity as a categorical, never as the label source
claim: Manufacturer, part number and memory type are worth encoding as categoricals and as interaction keys, but they must come from a static table that covers healthy units too.
rationale: The official data redacts manufacturing detail, Yu 2024 shows behaviour differing by platform, and the prior internal attempt found vendor/part grouping positive on its own ruler - while reading identity from the maintenance ticket, which only lists failed units.
applicability: Any fleet spanning more than one platform or vendor batch. Useless if the released identity column is a constant.
expected_effect: Small to medium; mostly it lets one model express per-platform thresholds.
risk: Deriving identity from the ticket makes it a direct label leak, and a batch identity that correlates with the collection period makes drift look like hardware quality.
impl_hint: join identity from a declared source keyed by unit id, assert coverage over the units without tickets before using the column, and keep the identity table out of any file that names individual units.

title: Aging and calendar drift are part of the signal, not noise
claim: Model time explicitly - unit age or first-seen-to-now, and the position of the prediction time inside the collection period - because hardware aging shifts the distribution between the training and the scoring window.
rationale: The competition README lists distribution shift due to hardware aging as one of the four named challenges; Yao 2021 raises long-term stability of the algorithm as a production requirement rather than a nice-to-have.
applicability: Splits that span months. Inside one week the calendar columns are constant and only add overfitting.
expected_effect: Uncertain: it can raise a time-extrapolation score or lower an in-period one, depending on which direction the drift runs.
risk: Calendar features let a model memorise the period it saw. A score that improves because the model learned 'this month is dangerous' will not carry to next month, and the audit cannot tell the two apart.
impl_hint: abstain by default and report the score with and without the time columns on the time-extrapolation split, rather than averaging the two configurations.

title: Bounded streaming over a 130 GB release
claim: Compute features in a bounded per-unit pass and persist intermediates in a columnar format: the same dataset is about 130 GB as csv and about 40 GB as feather, and the official pipeline runs per-unit work in parallel with chunked concatenation.
rationale: The starter-kit README states the two sizes and recommends the columnar form for processing; the baseline uses 16 worker processes, a per-SN file pass and chunked concat to bound memory.
applicability: Any run whose dataset does not fit in RAM several times over, which is the normal case here.
expected_effect: No direct score change; it is what makes the number of experiments per day large enough for a tournament to mean anything.
risk: A chunked pass must carry the lookback window across the boundary or rows get counted twice or dropped, so the chunked and whole-file paths must be proven equal rather than assumed equal.
impl_hint: read per unit, write one partition per bounded group of units keyed by the digest of the bytes written, and re-run only partitions whose digest changed.

title: Gradient-boosted trees on the sparse count features first
claim: Establish a LightGBM model over the tabular count features as the reference point before trying anything more expressive.
rationale: Both the starter kit and the published baseline train LightGBM; Yao 2021 reports a single gradient-boosted model placing 14th in a comparable production competition inside a 30 minute budget. The published criticism of automatic feature extraction is about extraction, not about trees.
applicability: Sparse integer count features with many zeros and a modest positive count, which is what the windowed representation produces.
expected_effect: Baseline quality; everything else is judged against it.
risk: On zero-heavy columns the model can learn 'this unit is quiet' as the dominant signal and rank an entire calendar period rather than a degraded unit, which a random split hides and a time split exposes.
impl_hint: keep NaN so the learner gets its own missing branch, cap the tree depth early, and hold the feature list in the run config so two comparisons differ in one thing only.

title: Per-platform model or pooled model, decided by measurement
claim: Compare a pooled model against per-platform models (or platform as an interaction feature) on the held-out period, because correctable-error semantics depend on how ECC is applied on a given architecture.
rationale: Yu 2024 compares x86 and ARM, finds platform-specific patterns, and reports up to 15 percent F1 from platform-aware modelling; the competition itself is built in two stages with an A/B list followed by mixed models to test exactly this.
applicability: Only where each platform holds enough failures to fit something; a rare platform modelled alone is fitting noise.
expected_effect: Medium when platforms are both distinct and well populated.
risk: Splitting multiplies the label-scarcity problem, and a platform key that also marks a collection period confuses heterogeneity with drift.
impl_hint: report the per-platform breakdown of the same score rather than one pooled number, so a gain on one queue cannot hide a loss on the other.

title: Learned spatial representations only after the tabular route is measured
claim: Treat per-level binary matrices with a learned spatial extractor, or sequence models over the event stream, as a second attempt that must beat the tuned tree model on the same split to be kept.
rationale: M2-MFP positions itself against rule-based models (low recall) and automatic feature extraction (suboptimal), and reports gains on production data - but its comparison is not against a strong tuned tree baseline on a time-extrapolation split.
applicability: Larger positive counts and a much bigger iteration budget than a tabular run needs.
expected_effect: Possible, unproven for this competition's setting.
risk: Harder to audit: a learned window built from an unsorted frame can read the future without any visible leakage rule being broken, and each iteration costs far more, which shrinks the number of comparisons behind the result.
impl_hint: if attempted, build tensors only from rows with time at or before the prediction time and re-run the same leakage audit that guards the tabular path.

title: Imbalance is a sampling design before it is a loss function
claim: Decide first which rows are eligible to be negatives, and only then weigh them: cap negative rows per healthy unit, restrict them to a follow-up-observed period, and keep the positive-to-negative unit ratio visible in the report.
rationale: Yao 2021 names extreme positive/negative imbalance as the central obstacle; the official baseline draws negatives from one contiguous 30-day block instead of the whole training period; the prior attempt capped healthy units at 200 sampled rows while leaving failed units uncapped, which it itself recorded as a covariate shift.
applicability: Every run on this data; uncorrected imbalance is the default failure mode.
expected_effect: Controls how many healthy units can be flagged at a fixed alert budget, which is the quantity the score is made of; no published delta exists for this dataset, so the effect is to be measured here rather than quoted.
risk: Row-level resampling changes which units dominate a unit-level metric, so a class weight that helps the row loss can hurt the ranking that is actually scored, and asymmetric capping between the two classes is a distribution shift of its own.
impl_hint: apply any per-unit row cap identically to both classes or state the asymmetry in the run config, and use the cap only for fast fixtures, never for the reported dev or val split.

title: Score is consumed as a ranking under an alert budget
claim: Optimise the top of the ranking: the operator replaces a bounded share of DIMMs, so precision within that budget decides the delivered value, and a probability calibrated to one period's prevalence does not transfer to the next.
rationale: The official F-score is written with a beta knob precisely so that precision-heavy settings are expressible; the only number the prior attempt was willing to quote publicly came from a one percent alert budget rather than from a probability threshold.
applicability: Whenever the threshold is chosen as a quantile of the score distribution rather than against a physical failure limit.
expected_effect: Changes what is optimised more than what is tuned: budget-based reporting usually moves the choice between two models that look equal on raw F1.
risk: Reporting calibration or precision on the same split that selected the threshold is self-serving, and a prevalence-calibrated probability is wrong by construction the moment the fleet composition changes.
impl_hint: report F1 at the chosen threshold plus precision at one and five percent of the fleet flagged, computed on a split whose scores never influenced the threshold.

title: The label window is fixed: lead 15 minutes, horizon 7 days
claim: A prediction made at time t is correct when the unit fails inside [t + 15 min, t + 15 min + 7 days]; both numbers come from the rules, not from tuning, and only the observation window before t is the participant's choice.
rationale: The competition homepage fixes the lead window at 15 minutes and the prediction window at 7 days; the README gives the observation / lead / prediction-period notation that makes the distinction explicit.
applicability: Every sample of every split, and the evaluator that scores the submission.
expected_effect: Not a performance feature: it defines which model is right.
risk: Any locally chosen window - a 10-day label span, or counting a failure that happened before t - silently changes the task, so a score computed under it cannot be compared with a score computed under the rules, and the difference is invisible in the number itself.
impl_hint: keep lead and horizon as declared configuration hashed into the run, and let the label window be derived from the prediction time rather than from the alarm time.

title: A negative is only a negative once its follow-up is observed
claim: Drop a sample whose label window reaches past the last observed instant instead of labelling it negative; the official baseline enforces this structurally by taking negatives from a 30-day block that ends 30 days before the training cutoff and by discarding tickets after the cutoff.
rationale: Read directly in the baseline's negative generator, and consistent with the fixed prediction horizon the homepage states: the buffer has to be at least the horizon for the label to be knowable.
applicability: Every grid whose period tail cannot yet be scored, which includes any recent data an operator would actually want to predict on.
expected_effect: Large on the estimate rather than on the model: un-censored tails turn the quietest region of the data into confirmed negatives and inflate recall claims.
risk: Failure-free units never appear in a ticket, so their coverage end has to come from somewhere else; inventing it per unit is a guess that no audit can see.
impl_hint: declare one coverage end for the run, require prediction time plus lead plus horizon to fall inside it, and count removed rows so a reviewer can see how much of the tail was unusable.

title: The baseline's positive definition is not a protocol to copy
claim: Do not reproduce the starter baseline's labelling as if it were the rules: it marks every feature row of a failing unit from 30 days before the alarm up to and including the alarm as positive, which labels rows three weeks from any failure as positives and rewards a model for approaching the alarm itself.
rationale: Read in the baseline's positive generator, and in direct conflict with the 15-minute lead and 7-day window the same documents state as the evaluation protocol.
applicability: Any reproduction of the starter kit or reuse of its training tables.
expected_effect: Avoids a specific trap rather than adding signal: the copied labelling scores well on a random split and badly on a time-extrapolation split.
risk: Scores computed on top of it are not comparable with anything else, and the confusion is attributed to the model rather than to the labels.
impl_hint: treat the starter kit as an engineering reference for features and formats, and take sampling, labelling and censoring from the protocol documents instead.

title: Grouping by unit is not the same as extrapolating in time
claim: Random per-unit K-fold compares models inside one calendar period. Score on a time-extrapolation split whose training side ends before the evaluation side, and purge or embargo every sample whose label window crosses the boundary.
rationale: The prior internal attempt used random per-unit folds and recorded that period-specific behaviour could not be separated out of its score; the leakage rule the repository now implements is a gap of at least lead plus horizon at every boundary.
applicability: Every comparison intended to predict next month, not last month.
expected_effect: Usually lowers the reported number. That is the point: the drop is what the old split was hiding.
risk: A unit present only in the evaluation period is unlearnable by definition, and a unit whose history straddles the boundary belongs to neither side; both need an explicit category rather than being quietly kept in train.
impl_hint: cut on prediction time with half-open intervals, embargo by lead plus horizon, and let an audit refuse the run when a split ends up empty or a cold unit sits in train.

title: The same physical error is logged many times
claim: Raw log counts are not error counts: de-duplicate a window by the position and parity signature before counting, the way the official baseline does, and keep that rule identical between the streaming and the whole-file path.
rationale: The baseline groups rows by position and parity, sums their Count and drops duplicates inside a window; without it a burst of identical reports reads as a storm.
applicability: Any window assembled from raw machine-check log lines.
expected_effect: Medium on the count features; it is a correction, not an addition.
risk: De-duplicating per chunk splits a duplicate pair across a boundary and re-introduces the double count, so a policy that is right once on a whole file can be wrong in a streaming implementation of the same file.
impl_hint: de-duplicate on the assembled window rather than the incoming chunk, and assert that the chunked and whole-file reads produce the same rows for the same unit.

title: An imputed sentinel is a value the model will split on
claim: Filling absent cells with a constant such as -1, as the baseline does, turns missingness into a magnitude: a tree can learn to split there, and any arithmetic on the column then mixes 'no data' with 'no errors'.
rationale: Read in the baseline configuration, whose imputation value is minus one. The released columns also carry an unknown or anonymised category, which is a second, different kind of missing.
applicability: Any feature derived from a column with sparse coverage.
expected_effect: Avoids a specific distortion; the effect size depends on how sparse it is.
risk: Keeping NaN instead produces different behaviour from the published baseline, so a reproduction attempt that changes both will not match and the reason will be invisible.
impl_hint: prefer NaN plus a separate explicit indicator for anonymised-but-present fields, and state in the run config which convention a comparison used.

title: Report the window-constrained score, not any-alarm ranking
claim: Score a prediction as correct only when an alarm for that unit falls inside the labelled window, and report that strict number alongside the looser unit-ranking number; a metric that only asks whether the unit ever appears near the top of the list is an upper bound.
rationale: The rules define true positives through the prediction period relative to each prediction time, while aggregating row scores into one unit score drops the timing that makes the strict definition checkable - the prior attempt kept both rulers precisely because the loose one read better.
applicability: Every report, demo and submission in this task.
expected_effect: Typically a large downward correction of the headline number, and no change to the model.
risk: Publishing only the loose figure makes a genuine improvement look like the protocol was changed to flatter it.
impl_hint: aggregate row scores per unit with their timestamps attached, and print both scores from one run so a reviewer cannot be handed only the flattering one.

title: A number under a changed protocol is not an improvement
claim: Never present a score computed under the new sampling, labelling or aggregation rules as a gain over a score computed under the old ones; the leaderboard being closed removes the one external calibration that could settle the comparison.
rationale: The prior attempt's quotable figure came from a 10-day soft label, alarm-anchored sampling and a threshold swept on the evaluation scores; the competition record shows the phase ended, so no new submission can be checked against the official evaluator.
applicability: Every claim in a report, README or pull request in this phase.
expected_effect: Protects the credibility of every other number.
risk: The honest alternative - re-running the old method under the new rules - costs a full pipeline run, which is exactly why it gets skipped.
impl_hint: state the protocol version with each score, and label any historical figure as historical reference rather than as a baseline.

title: Choose the threshold inside the training period, or fix a budget
claim: Select the operating threshold from cross-validation over earlier time only, or fix it in advance as an alert-budget quantile; sweeping quantiles over the evaluation scores turns the reported absolute number into an upper bound.
rationale: The prior attempt swept 60 quantiles of its own out-of-fold evaluation scores and recorded the result as a known optimism in its own report; the official metric depends on the threshold through both precision and recall, so the choice is part of the result.
applicability: Any thresholded F1, which is every number this task produces.
expected_effect: Usually a downward correction of the headline score, sometimes a large one.
risk: A threshold tuned on the training period can be badly placed after drift, which is why a fixed-budget operating point should be reported next to the tuned one.
impl_hint: fit the threshold inside a time-ordered inner loop, freeze it, and score the held-out period once with that frozen value.

title: Treat the two released queues as two domains
claim: Measure what a model trained on one released queue does on the other before deciding whether to pool them, since the queues differ in their available columns and in how many units each holds.
rationale: The competition is organised as an A/B list in stage one and a deliberately mixed dataset in stage two to test transfer; Yu 2024 shows failure patterns moving with the platform; the prior attempt measured per-platform segmentation as helpful on its own ruler and found the two queues shipped different precomputed feature widths.
applicability: Any run whose data is partitioned by platform, batch or collection host.
expected_effect: Decides the model's shape: one model, two models, or one plus an adapter.
risk: Pooling hides a queue that is much harder; separating hides a queue too small to fit; and a column present in only one queue becomes an all-missing feature in the other, which is the sentinel problem rather than a transfer result.
impl_hint: train on queue one and score on queue two as its own reported split, with the feature intersection used so a missing column cannot look like a transfer result.
